# RetailCast India — Approach Summary / Technical Decision Log

*(~1,480 words. Every claim is regenerated by `src/audit.py`; the model by `src/forecast.py`.)*

## Q1. Audit method (~150 words)

I audited provenance before performance, in five passes. **(1) Coverage/shape:** day-range of every file, confirming `sales` and `market_signal` stop at `d_1913` while `calendar`, `sell_prices` and `vendor_signal` reach the horizon. **(2) Feed provenance:** for each vendor feed I correlated its value against actual `units` at time lags −2…+2, checked its behaviour on zero-sales days, and its value/units ratio — the test for whether a "signal" is a leading indicator or a disguised copy of the target. **(3) Backtest of the vendor forecast** against trailing-mean and seasonal baselines on held-out history. **(4) Per-series/per-store regime scan:** prior-year vs last-90-day level, births/deaths, breakpoints. **(5) Feature usefulness:** within-series price/units correlation, festival uplift, weekday profile. I stopped when each candidate feature had a keep/drop decision backed by a number, and every regime flag was cross-checked against sibling series.

## Q2. Data verdicts (~500 words)

**V1 — `market_signal.csv` is target leakage and unavailable at prediction time.**
*What:* all 60 series, `d_1`–`d_1913` only. *Evidence:* mean per-series `corr(units, mkt_signal)` = **0.92 at lag 0**, collapsing to **0.37 at lag ±1**; `mkt_signal` is **exactly 0 in 100%** of zero-sales rows and never 0 when `units>0`; the value/units ratio is ~10 with noise (so `mkt_signal ≈ units × 10 × ε`). It also ends at `d_1913`, so it does not exist for `d_1914`–`d_1941`. *Action:* excluded entirely. *Rejected reading:* "a leading demand index worth forecasting forward." Ruled out because a genuine leading indicator peaks at a **positive** lag, not lag 0, and would not be identically zero exactly when sales are zero — that is contemporaneous target contamination, and there is nothing to join to on the horizon anyway.

**V2 — `vendor_signal.csv` is legitimate but too weak to trust as the forecast.**
*What:* all 60 series, `d_1`–`d_1941` (covers the horizon). *Evidence:* never exactly 0 on zero-sales days (mean 3.9), weak within-series day-to-day corr (0.12); on a last-28-day backtest its **per-series WAPE = 1.04 vs 0.82** for a plain trailing-28-day mean. *Action:* not used as the forecast; kept only as an optional inspection/blend anchor. *Rejected reading:* "a vendor baseline is safe to submit or to weight heavily." Ruled out by the backtest — a free trailing mean beats it per series, so leaning on it would import error.

**V3 — Store `KA_3` is in a real, store-wide demand decline (regime change).**
*What:* all six `KA_3` series (`ELECTRONICS_1_CABLE/CHARGER`, `HOMECARE_1_DETERGENT`, `HOMECARE_2_AGARBATTI`, `GROCERY_3_ATTA/PICKLE`), over roughly the **last 100 days (≈ d_1815–d_1913)**. *Evidence:* last-90-day mean is **0.25–0.49× the prior-year mean** for the five meaningful-volume series; the same products in other stores hold ~1.0 (e.g. `HOMECARE_1_DETERGENT`: KA_3 ratio 0.25 vs 0.69–1.90 elsewhere). Rolling-60 means slide monotonically from ~d_1800. *Action:* for `KA_3` the level uses a **28-day window** (vs 42 elsewhere) so the forecast sits on the current regime, not an average dragged up by 2022. *Rejected reading:* "random dip / noise in a few SKUs." Ruled out because the drop is coherent across **all six** products in the one store and monotone, i.e. a store-level cause (footfall/closure), not per-SKU sampling noise.

**V4 — `HOMECARE_2_AGARBATTI_MH_4` is a late introduction.**
*What:* first non-zero sale at `d_268`. *Evidence:* `d_1`–`d_267` are all zero, then normal intermittent sales. *Action:* the recent-window level ignores the pre-introduction zeros automatically, so no full-history mean is polluted. *Rejected reading:* "a dead/erroneous series to drop" — ruled out because it sells normally after introduction.

## Q3. What I left alone (~150 words)

I deliberately did **not** clip the large festival spikes — e.g. `GROCERY_3_ATTA_MH_3` = **612 units on d_303 (Diwali, 2018-11-04)**, ~5× the series' positive-day median, and matching Diwali spikes in the other ATTA stores. Statistically these are extreme outliers, and a naive "winsorise the top 1%" step would remove them. That would be wrong: they are genuine, recurring festival demand, and the horizon itself contains festivals (Ram Navami, Eid). Clipping real seasonal peaks would bias festival-period forecasts low. My restraint is safe here specifically because the spikes are **old (2018–2020) and far from the horizon**, and my level comes from a 42-/28-day recent window — so they inform the day-of-week/festival structure without distorting the level. I treat them as signal to learn from, not error to erase.

## Q4. Modelling choices (~250 words)

**Final model (per series):** `forecast = recent_level × day-of-week multiplier × festival uplift`, clipped at 0. Level = mean of the last 42 days (28 for `KA_3`); the DOW profile comes from the last 180 days (weekend lift is real: Sat 15.7 vs Tue 9.3 pooled); festival days get 1.15× (measured uplift ~1.3×, discounted to avoid over-fitting sparse events).

**How Q2 shaped it:** V1 → `market_signal` excluded; V2 → `vendor_signal` not used; V3 → the short, per-store-adaptive window is the mechanism that respects the KA_3 regime, so regime information enters through *estimation window*, not a dummy; near-zero price elasticity (median corr −0.03) → price excluded.

**Considered and rejected:** (a) a pooled gradient-boosted model with lag/rolling features — rejected because it would happily ingest the leaked `market_signal`, and the KA_3 break makes global lag features misleading; high overfitting risk against a horizon the brief says is noise-floored. (b) Per-series ETS/ARIMA — reasonable, but with 14 highly intermittent series (>70% zeros) and short usable regime windows, it adds fragility for no backtest gain. (c) Submitting `vendor_forecast` — rejected by V2's backtest. (d) A vendor blend — tested; it did not beat the recency model on either holdout, so it was dropped for simplicity. The rubric's flat accuracy curve rewards a robust, honest baseline over a fragile "clever" one.

## Q5. Validation I trust (~200 words)

I used **two rolling 28-day holdouts**: train on `≤ d_1857` and score `d_1858–d_1885`, then train on `≤ d_1885` and score `d_1886–d_1913`. I scored exactly the competition metrics — **mean RMSSE** (per-series, scaled by the in-sample 1-step naive error) and volume-weighted **WAPE**. Results: RMSSE **0.819 / 0.828**, WAPE **0.398 / 0.366**. I **expected horizon mean RMSSE ≈ 0.83–0.90** and WAPE ≈ 0.38–0.43.

Why it is honest: every backtest forecast is built only from data before its cut — the leaked `market_signal` is never used, so no optimistic contamination. The main way local validation could flatter reality is that both holdouts fall in Feb–Apr, while the true horizon (Apr) contains two festivals my 1.15× factor only approximates; and the KA_3 decline could steepen beyond what a held level predicts. I widened the expected range upward to reflect that, rather than quoting the rosier 0.82. Using two windows (not one) guards against tuning the window length to a single lucky month.

## Q6. Least-sure call (~150 words)

The `KA_3` treatment. I **hold** the recent (28-day) level flat across the horizon rather than extrapolating the observed decline. If the store is still sliding, I will over-forecast KA_3 for a second time; if the decline has bottomed out, extrapolating down would have over-corrected. With one more day I would fit a short local trend on the last ~60 KA_3 days and test, on the d_1886–d_1913 holdout, whether a gentle downward slope beats a held level — the evidence that would move me is a statistically clear negative slope that *continues* through the holdout rather than flattening. I hedged by choosing the shorter 28-day window (which already leans the level down toward the current regime) but stopping short of projecting further decline, because over-extrapolating a trend into a 28-day horizon is the more common and more damaging error.

## Q7. Reproduce and stress (~100 words)

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt && python src/forecast.py --data data --out submission.csv
```

Would the pipeline catch a *new* problem of the same family next month? **Partly, and honestly not fully automatically.** The recency window self-heals a *new* regime shift (a different store declining) without code changes, because the level always tracks recent days — that generalises. But it would **not** automatically flag a *new leaked feed*: `market_signal` is excluded by name, so a differently-named contaminated feed would need me to re-run `audit.py`'s lag-0/zero-day test. So: regime changes — the pipeline. New leakage — me, via the audit. I'd wire the lag-0 correlation and zero-day checks into a pre-flight assertion to close that gap.
